## Problem
`planko_list_notes` didn't expose `dueDateFrom`/`dueDateTo`, so notes couldn't be listed by day/range. Since the backend applies the recurring-copy exclusion **only when there's no date filter**, a notes-by-day request (which never carried a date filter) returned an empty list for users whose daily notes are recurring occurrences.

## Fix
- Add `dueDateFrom`/`dueDateTo` to `planko_list_notes` (mirrors `planko_list_tasks`). `buildListParams` already forwards any declared param, so no other plumbing changes.
- Correct the tool description: recurring notes show as one entry per series **unless** a due-date range is given, in which case the individual dated occurrences are returned.

Everything else on `list_notes` is intentionally unchanged — `status`/`showCompleted` already cover completed filtering; `priority`/`parentId` are task concepts and stay omitted.

## Pairs with
planko-back **#318** (backend gates the recurring-copy exclusion on the date filter). Both are needed for notes-by-day to work end to end.

author: pablomoli
body:
## The defect

`MasonryGrid`'s layout effect depended on `children`, which React allocates fresh on every parent render, so `Object.is` always failed. The grid re-packed and re-tweened every card whenever anything on the page changed — a selection toggle, a react-query poll, or the inbox's 1s elapsed clock during an ingest job.

Selecting a card cannot move anything: `.card.selected` is a pure `outline-color` change, and outline does not participate in layout. Yet one click rewrote the position of all 60 cards.

## Evidence

Measured against the live inbox at 60 cards, counting `style` attribute writes on the grid's children through a `MutationObserver`. Left arm is the installed hub on :6969, right arm is this branch's dev server, same data:

|                          | before | after |
|--------------------------|-------:|------:|
| idle 6s, no interaction  |      0 |     0 |
| one card click           |  1,286 |     0 |
| five card clicks         |  6,430 |     0 |
| viewport resize          |    173 |   173 |

The resize row is the control. Real geometry changes still repack exactly as before — this removes the unprovoked passes, not the layout.

## What changed

- **Trigger.** The effect depends on a structural signature (the ordered card keys) instead of children identity. Membership and order are the only things that can change the packing, and both are visible in that signature.
- **Measurement.** The `ResizeObserver` now watches each card as well as the grid. Anything that changes a card's height — an image decoding, an errored cover falling back to text, a font landing — reaches the layout through measurement rather than through a re-render. This is what makes dropping the per-render pass safe; without it, a cover falling back to `.noimg` would have left a stale height.
- **Idempotence.** A pass that would write the geometry each card already has returns without writing or animating. The comparison is against the DOM, not against the previous placement list: a reorder produces the *same* list of positions handed to *different* cards, and keying on the list alone left every card at its predecessor's coordinates. The reorder test caught this.

Motion is now reserved for structural change. Resizes and late image loads snap, as they did before.

## Why it hid for months

Reduced motion only skipped the GSAP tween. The repack still ran, silently and instantly — so full motion showed a flicker and reduced motion showed content quietly relocated. Same defect, evidence removed. That is the inverse of #124, where reduced motion *revealed* text full motion left unreadable, and it is why #21 now carries a standing rule that motion state must never determine whether a defect is observable.

Verified: full and reduced motion produce identical geometry (60 cards, 5218px container, zero differing positions).

## Tests

Five regression tests on the trigger, all failing before the fix on the two that encode the bug:

- a parent re-render with the same cards does not animate
- re-rendering ten times over never accumulates animations (stands in for the ingest clock)
- adding a card animates the reflow
- reordering the same cards animates the reflow
- every card still gets placed after a no-op re-render

Full suite: 48 files, 177 tests passing. `tsc -b` clean. `vp lint` back to the two pre-existing `exhaustive-deps` warnings documented in #122 — no findings in the changed files.

## Not in scope

The inbox's 1s elapsed clock still lives in the component that renders the cards (#22 mechanism 3). With the trigger fixed it is no longer a correctness problem, only a wasted render, so moving it belongs with the rail work in #125. Reserving image boxes with `aspect-ratio` so the first layout measures true heights is the remaining half of #22 and is worth its own change.

Closes #22

author: galletas1712
body:
Stacked on #305 — base is `feature/concurrent-delegations`, so this diff shows only the follow-up work.

A detailed review of #305 raised 11 issues. This fixes all of them.

## Blocking issue found during review

The prompt migration originally added here rewrote **every** session whose stored prompt still carried the pre-concurrency delegation rules. Against the live database that is 972 rows — but **788 of them are subagent sessions**, created before parent/subagent prompt profiles were split, which embed the parent delegation block verbatim. The migration would have told historical subagents they may "launch several independent delegations… up to eight read-only slots", which is wrong: subagents have no delegation tools.

The rewrite is now scoped with `parent_session_id is null`, and the post-condition assertion is scoped identically (otherwise the untouched subagent rows would trip it and abort the whole migration).

## Changes

**Dead code / test-only production APIs**
- Delete `list_parent_delegations_newest`, `set_delegation_status`, `cancel_running_delegation_and_queued_partials`. Every test caller moves onto the real transitions (`finish_delegation`, `begin_`/`finish_delegation_teardown`). Several tests are now stronger, because those APIs enforce readiness preconditions the forced status bypassed.
- Delete the legacy `create_delegation` wrapper, which fabricated launch shapes (hardcoded `"implementer"` / `"reviewer"`) on a production path.

**Correctness / consistency**
- Collapse the duplicated session task-abort body onto one primitive.
- Run `reconcile_partial_launches_on_boot` exactly once per boot instead of twice.
- Namespace the production launch key as `action:{row_id}`; every producer is now namespaced.
- Express the terminal handoff-artifact policy once in `handoff.rs`.

**Documentation** — corrects claims that were misleading or already rotten
- `.pi-handoff`: describe the real mechanism. A btrfs subvolume snapshot has no exclude facility, so the child cwd is snapshotted and the directory removed immediately under the per-cwd mutation guard. The previous "excluded from every fork" phrasing is exactly what rotted into a false claim when #287 dropped the real exclusion.
- `handoff_dir` is stated plainly as cwd-relative; it always was, and presenting it as changed behaviour was wrong.
- Document that `history.fork` no longer inherits `.pi-handoff`.
- Document the `input.follow_up` `accepted`/`queued`/`replayed` derivation.
- Record two known limitations: the startup check validates index *validity*, not *definition*; and the 8-slot read-only cap rests on the parent row lock with no unique-index backstop, unlike writer exclusivity.

**Tests**
- Cover the follow-up response shape, boot ordering, and the prompt migration against partial-fragment and legacy subagent prompts.
- Add a btrfs-gated regression test for the `.pi-handoff` fork removal (gated on `PI_RELAY_TEST_BTRFS_ROOT`).
- The prompt-migration test no longer derives its seed by inverting the migration's own constants — it uses a checked-in literal of the real pre-concurrency block, so the test cannot pass by sharing a bug with the SQL.

## New migration step

`rust/migrations/concurrent-delegations-prompts.sql` is a **third** one-time script, added to the runbook in `rust/migrations/README.md`. It runs after the control plane is stopped and before new binaries are deployed.

It removes the pre-concurrency single-delegation instruction from every top-level prompt so no stored prompt contradicts the concurrent tool schemas. It does **not** regenerate whole prompts: most stored prompts predate the current `PI.md`, so they keep their older surrounding prose.

Verified against a 680-row seeded copy of the real prompt corpus on a throwaway Postgres:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Run 1 | exit 0, rewrote 250 rows (0 subagents) |
| Subagent rows changed (n=400, md5) | 0, byte-identical |
| Top-level rows with any stale fragment | 0 |
| Double-appends | 0 |
| Run 2 | exit 0, 0 rows changed |

## Validation

- `agent-store`: 85 passed, 0 failed (real PostgreSQL, `--include-ignored`)
- `agent-daemon`: 213 passed, 0 failed (real PostgreSQL, `--include-ignored`)
- `cargo check --all --all-targets`: clean
- clippy: clean apart from one pre-existing `items_after_test_module` warning in untouched code
- web: 554 tests passed, `tsc --noEmit` clean

Two reviewers went over this: code/concurrency **approved**; migration/docs requested the scoping change above, which is now applied.

## Breaking changes

1. `input.follow_up` always returns `replayed`, and `accepted`/`queued` derive from the stored row status rather than being hardcoded `true`.
2. `history.fork` no longer inherits `.pi-handoff`, so a forked session starts with no delegation artifact history.
3. Production launch keys move from a bare `row_id` to `action:{row_id}`. Safe, because `concurrent-delegations.sql` rewrites all pre-existing rows to `legacy:{id}`.

## Not done

The btrfs fork test was verified on a btrfs host by the implementer but not re-run by the reviewer, who had no btrfs available. Worth one run before merge.

body:
## What

Comments and docs only — no behaviour change. Typecheck clean; full suite passes (**580 passed, 13 skipped**; the 2 skipped files are the build-gated and DB-gated integration tests).

Follow-up to #142. That PR rebuilt the runbook; this one fixes the claims the same walkthrough falsified **in code and in ADR-011**, which #142 deliberately left alone to keep the diff reviewable.

## Why this isn't cosmetic

Three of these were assertions a future reader would have trusted:

| Claim | Reality | Where it lived |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Attack-traffic cost is "bounded by an explicit Neon spend threshold (D6)" | **No threshold exists or can be set** — Free plan has no balance. Bounded by Free's hard caps instead, and **that bound vanishes on upgrade** | `auth.ts:68-71`, ADR-011 D5/D6 |
| `neondb_owner` rotates "after the injected set is removed" | Rotating **re-triggers the sync and re-injects all 18 vars** — the two halves cancel | ADR-011 D9 |
| Five app secrets in the web project, incl. `PROJECTION_WRITE_DATABASE_URL` | That's the **write** credential; ADR-007 forbids the web runtime holding it. Found live in Production, removed. Four secrets | ADR-011 D2 |
| D7's 30-day session is safe because revocation is pullable in under a minute | It **wasn't** — no credential on the machine could reach `numisma_auth`; `vercel env pull` returns sensitive vars as empty strings, silently | ADR-011 D7 |

**No decision is reversed.** Each intent stands; the amendment records the gap between a decision and the mechanism claimed to implement it — which is exactly where stale documentation does damage.

## Approach

ADR-011 is **amended, not rewritten**, following ADR-007's existing convention (`## Amendment: …`, status line updated). Inline `⚠` markers at D2, D5, and D6 point at the amendment so a reader landing mid-document doesn't miss it.

## Also

- `.env.example` gains two notes **next to the connection strings**: hosted values aren't sourceable from Vercel (and the failure is silent), and `pg` v9 will **weaken** `sslmode=require`, which today aliases `verify-full`. That one has no test and no error — the strings just stop validating certificates.
- `client-bundle.integration.test.ts`'s `VITE_NEON_AUTH_URL` exclusion is re-justified: it was defended as shipping for "a working feature" that never existed, and the variable is now gone entirely.

## Test plan

`pnpm --filter @numisma/web typecheck` and `pnpm test`. Nothing else — every change is a comment or a markdown document.

author: villebro
body:
## Summary

Renovate's dependency dashboard flags `github.com/robfig/cron/v3` as stale — its last commit was in early 2021 and there have been no releases since. This PR replaces it with the actively-maintained [`github.com/adhocore/gronx`](https://github.com/adhocore/gronx) (MIT, last release 2026), which removes `robfig/cron/v3` from the module graph entirely.

While swapping the library, this also **expands** cron support to everything gronx offers: in addition to the classic 5-field form, `cronSchedule` now accepts an optional leading **seconds** field and/or trailing **year** field (6- or 7-field expressions, e.g. `*/30 * * * * *` every 30 seconds, `0 0 2 * * * 2027`). Existing 5-field schedules parse and compute identical ticks, so this is **additive, not breaking**.

`go-co-op/gocron` was considered but rejected: it is a job *scheduler* (wrong shape for our pure requeue-timing math) and it depends on `robfig/cron/v3` internally, so it would not clear the staleness flag.

## Details

- **`internal/schedule/schedule.go`** — rewritten on gronx: `CurrentTick` → `PrevTickBefore(expr, now, true)` (inclusive prev tick), `NextTick` → `NextTickAfter(expr, now, false)` (strictly after), `Validate` → `IsValid`. The hand-rolled `findPrevTick` geometric-doubling loop is deleted — gronx has native previous-tick support.
- **`api/v1alpha1/superset_types.go`** — the `cronSchedule` CEL pattern is relaxed from exactly 5 fields (`{4}`) to 5–7 fields (`{4,6}`), and the field doc updated. Deep per-field range validation is still handled at runtime by `gronx.IsValid`, and the existing `gateOnInvalidSeedSchedule` runtime gate remains the backstop for out-of-range values that pass the coarse admission pattern.
- **Generated artifacts** — CRD YAML, Helm CRDs, and `docs/reference/api-reference.md` regenerated via `make codegen`.
- **Docs** — `docs/user-guide/lifecycle.md` wording updated; changelog entry added under **Added**.
- **Tests** — all existing `internal/schedule` tests pass unchanged (semantic-equivalence acceptance criteria); added outcome tests for 6-field seconds and 7-field year expressions.

## Verification

- `make test-unit` passes (`internal/schedule` 100% coverage, `internal/controller` unaffected)
- `make lint` — golangci-lint reports 0 issues
- `make codegen` is idempotent (no drift); regenerated CRD carries the `{4,6}` pattern
- `robfig/cron` no longer appears anywhere in the tree

body:
## Summary

- return bare S3 paste IDs from expiration scans so configured prefixes are applied exactly once during deletion
- stop S3 and Google Cloud scans at the documented batch size instead of one item later
- ignore nested discussion/config objects when selecting expired top-level pastes
- require enumerated and purge-candidate cloud paste IDs to match the model's 16-hex format
- store Google Cloud salt and limiter objects beneath the configured prefix
- copy legacy unprefixed Google Cloud config into the prefix on first access

## Reproduction

With the default non-empty S3 prefix, an expired object named `pastes/<id>` was returned as the paste ID. `delete()` then applied the prefix again and targeted `pastes/pastes/<id>`, leaving the expired paste in storage.

Both cloud implementations also used `count($expired) > $batchsize`, allowing a purge configured for two items to return and delete three.

Google Cloud applied its configured prefix to paste objects but always stored salts and limiter state under the shared `config/` path. Two PrivateBin instances using different prefixes in one bucket therefore overwrote each other's server salt, traffic limiter, and purge limiter.

Both cloud backends also treated any top-level object beneath the prefix as a paste. Names such as `not-a-paste` and `<id>.backup` appeared in administration/migration enumeration and could consume the purge batch before real expired pastes were selected.

The new S3 regression starts with three expired `pastes/<id>` objects and verifies that `purge(2)` deletes exactly:

```text
pastes/aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa
pastes/bbbbbbbbbbbbbbbb
```

## Tests

- `phpunit Data/S3StorageTest.php` — 1 test, 2 assertions passed
- `php -d auto_prepend_file=/tmp/privatebin-google.ABreG0/vendor/autoload.php /usr/bin/phpunit Data/GoogleCloudStorageTest.php`
  - 9 tests, 88 assertions passed
- `php -d auto_prepend_file=/tmp/privatebin-google.ABreG0/vendor/autoload.php /usr/bin/phpunit --filter '/^(?!.*ServerSaltTest)/'`
  - 270 tests, 6522 assertions passed
- PHP syntax checks for both implementations and test files
- `composer validate --no-check-publish`

## Compatibility and privacy

Fresh Google Cloud installations keep configuration state isolated by prefix. On upgrade, a missing prefixed value falls back to the legacy unprefixed object and copies it into the prefix before returning it, preserving existing deletion tokens. The shared legacy object is not removed because another configured prefix may not have migrated yet. Enumeration and purge now operate only on IDs that normal model methods can address. No paste ciphertext or metadata is moved.

## AI/LLM disclosure

This change was investigated, implemented, and tested with OpenAI Codex assistance. The commits and test evidence are included in this draft for manual review.

body:
`bench.yml` and `query-bench.yml` both target the same self-hosted `[Linux]` runner. Their existing concurrency groups are keyed per PR, so two PRs (or bench + query-bench on one PR) could benchmark simultaneously and measure each other's load.

Adds a job-level concurrency group shared by both workflows:

```yaml
concurrency:
  group: bench-runner
  cancel-in-progress: false
```

Layered on top of the unchanged workflow-level per-PR groups:

- **workflow level** — `bench-<PR#>`, `cancel-in-progress: true`: a new push still cancels its own stale run.
- **job level** — one `bench-runner` group, no cancellation: everything else queues and runs one at a time.

Caveat: GitHub keeps only one pending run per concurrency group. If a third bench job arrives while one is running and one is queued, the queued one is cancelled and its report never posts. Fine at current PR volume; if it bites, the alternative is dropping the job-level group and dedicating a single self-hosted runner label instead, which serializes without the pending-slot limit.

## Root cause

The TCP keyboard/control path could recover independently while the UDP/I²S/Core Audio path remained falsely online. author: mparrett
body:
`10n.toString()` prints nothing and exits 0. So do `valueOf()`, `toLocaleString()`, and `BigInt(10n)` — every BigInt prototype method is unusable on a primitive receiver.

Two commits: the panic fix, and a separable radix fix that the first one makes reachable.

## 1. The panic

All four sites inlined the same object-wrapper unwrap:

```go
if v.Type() == vm.TypeBigInt {
    // For BigInt object wrappers, extract the primitive value from [[BigIntData]]
    if po := v.AsPlainObject(); po != nil {
```

`AsPlainObject` panics unless the value is `TypeObject` (`value.go:968-971`), and a BigInt object wrapper *is* `TypeObject` — never `TypeBigInt`. The guard admits exactly the values the body cannot handle: the wrapper branch was unreachable, and every primitive receiver panicked.

It reads as a silent stop rather than a crash because `VM.run`'s recover discards the panic and returns `InterpretOK` — filed separately as #44.

Replaced all four copies with one `thisBigIntValue` helper implementing ThisBigIntValue. Four hand-inlined copies of a subtle unwrap is what produced four identical bugs.

**The slot name matters here.** The spec calls it `[[BigIntData]]`, and that is what the old code looked up — but nothing in this repo ever writes that name. `Object(bigint)` stores `[[PrimitiveValue]]` (`object_init.go:944`), so searching for the spec name would have left the wrapper arm dead in a new place. The helper uses `[[PrimitiveValue]]` and checks the stored value's type, since Number/String/Boolean/Symbol wrappers share that slot.

## 2. The radix

`toString`'s radix was coerced with a bare `ToFloat` and clamped into 2..36, with a comment noting real JS throws. Now runs the package's existing `toIntegerOrInfinityWithVM` and throws `RangeError` outside 2..36.

Separable, but included because commit 1 is what makes these paths reachable — see the test262 accounting below. Happy to split it out if you'd rather.

## Verification

Primitive and wrapper receivers, all matching Node:

```
10n.toString()                          10
10n.toString(16)                        a
BigInt("-255").toString(16)             -ff
10n.valueOf()                           10n   (typeof bigint)
10n.toLocaleString()                    10
BigInt(10n)                             10n
Object(10n).toString()                  10
Object(10n).toLocaleString()            10
BigInt.prototype.valueOf.call(Object(10n))  10n
BigInt(Object(10n))                     10n
```

Non-BigInt receiver fallbacks are unchanged: `toString`/`toLocaleString` stringify, `valueOf` throws `TypeError`.

`tests/scripts/bigint_prototype_methods.ts` covers all of the above. With commit 1 reverted it fails with `"undefined"` — the script produces nothing at all.

`go build`/`vet`/`gofmt` clean; `TestScripts`, `pkg/vm`, `pkg/builtins`, `pkg/compiler` pass.

### test262

`built-ins/BigInt`: **41 → 41**, and `language`: 23222/23648 with zero per-test diffs.

The count is flat but the composition changed, so the per-test diff is worth stating plainly:

- **+1** `prototype/valueOf/cross-realm.js` — genuinely fixed by the wrapper unwrap.
- **−1** `prototype/toString/radix-tointegerorinfinity-throws-toprimitive-or-bigint.js` — this was a false pass. The panic ended the script before its assertion ran, and the harness scored the silence as green. It now fails for a real, pre-existing reason: `toIntegerOrInfinityWithVM` doesn't reject a BigInt returned from `ToPrimitive`. That helper is shared with Array, so fixing it belongs in its own change where the Array impact can be measured — deliberately not touched here.

Two other radix tests (`radix-err.js`, `radix-tointegerorinfinity-throws-symbol.js`) were false passes for the same reason; commit 2 turns those into genuine passes, which is why the total lands back at 41 rather than 38.

## Note on the test

It calls through `any`. The checker rejects property access on a bigint receiver outright ("property access is not supported on type bigint"), rejects unary `-` on bigint, and types a bigint literal as a number literal (`const b: bigint = 10n` fails). All pre-existing and unrelated to this PR — happy to file separately if you want them tracked.

author: swalha1999
body:
Everything ContextBridge did until now was configuration and a status line. This slice is the part a **person** touches: eleven words — `status`, `search`, `flush`, `pause`, `resume`, `remember`, `sync`, `rebuild`, `retry`, `doctor`, `help` — on two surfaces that share one implementation, so `/cb flush` in a chat and `contextbridge flush` in a terminal cannot come to mean different things.

**Nothing changes for an install that types nothing.** No new configuration key, no new opt-in, no behaviour change to retrieval, capture, reconciling, applying or synchronizing. Schema version 5 adds one table and alters nothing.

**Nothing model-facing is added.** `ctx.register_tool` is still never called; the fake context in the tests still fails loudly if it ever is. What a person can type and what the model can call are different promises, and only the first is made here.

## What is in it

* **`/cb`**, through the host's public `ctx.register_command` (`fn(raw_args: str) -> str | None`). The handler always answers with a string, catches everything, and is bounded: reads, one small transaction, at most one index rebuild. A host that refuses the registration costs nothing.
* **`contextbridge <command>`** with `--hermes-home` for choosing a profile the way Hermes chooses one. A home that is not already there is refused rather than created. Exit codes: `0` fine, `1` refused or degraded, `2` mistyped or unloadable configuration.
* **A compact, schema-versioned report.** `status --json` is a document with `schema_version: 1`, deterministic (every age comes from an injected clock) and content-free: repository revision/branch health, retrieval and index state with the token budget, queue counts, reconciler mode with staged counts and last stable reason codes, sync state with unpushed count and last-success age. It carries this plugin's own paths and **not** the context repository's; the compact rendering `/cb` posts carries no path at all. `status --full` is the long operator report, which is where paths belong.
* **`doctor`**, human and `--json` (`schema_version: 1`): sixteen checks, all reported every time so the document has one shape. `--fix` repairs exactly five things — an expired lease, a damaged index, an orphaned or half-written journal, our own `.cbtmp-` files under the data directory, our own 0700/0600 modes — and answers `refused` to everything else, including our own temporary files when they were left *inside* the repository.
* **Pausing as a scope**: `pause` holds reconciling, applying and synchronizing; `pause all` also stops injecting and capturing, from the next turn rather than the next restart. It lives in `queue.db`, so a pause typed in a gateway is honoured by whichever process holds the worker's lease.
* **`remember`**, through the capture path's own redaction, length cap, sentinel refusal and deterministic event id — storing the request with the words, which is what makes it explicit to the gate rather than inferred.
* **`search`**, which answers *where* (document and heading) and never *what*. It builds nothing: an absent index is reported.

## The two rules that shape it

**A control asks; the worker acts.** Flushing starts a batch that calls a model and synchronizing reaches a remote, so both record a request and return — nothing a person types runs a model call, a fetch or a push inside somebody's turn. No control takes the profile's single-writer lock, because none of them writes to the repository.

**The two sides fail in opposite directions, on purpose.** The worker fails **closed**: a control state it cannot read is treated as paused, because committing and pushing through an unreadable pause is the mistake a pause exists to prevent. The hooks fail **open**: there the cost of guessing wrong is a row nobody reads, and the cost of raising is the user's turn. A paused profile still *recovers* an interrupted apply, because a half-written repository is worse than either outcome.

## Host limitation, verified rather than assumed

`tests/integration/test_real_hermes_commands.py` runs against the pinned Hermes v0.19.0 checkout:

* `register_command` **silently drops** a name that collides with a built-in, so the name is checked against the host's real registry. `cb` is free; the test also proves what a collision would have done.
* `/context` is unclaimed today and is still not taken: it is the most generic word in a product about context, and a Hermes that later claimed it would silently disable this plugin's only in-session surface.
* **`hermes context …` is a deliberate absence.** `ctx.register_cli_command` exists and `context` is not a built-in subcommand, so it *would* register — but reaching it requires the host to **load** the plugin, and loading initializes the profile's queue, which would make `status` and `doctor` create the state they promise only to report. Plugin CLI commands are also absent from `hermes --help` by design in this host, and a generic name squatted in a shared argparse tree would break every plugin's CLI registration if Hermes later claimed it. The console script needs no host at all.

## Verification

All seven pre-proposal gates from `AGENTS.md`, run with a fresh temporary `HERMES_HOME` and the pinned `HERMES_TESTBED`:

| Gate | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `uv run pytest --cov=contextbridge --cov-report=term-missing` | **2592 passed**, **100.00%** statement *and* branch coverage |
| `uv run ruff format --check .` | 137 files already formatted |
| `uv run ruff check .` | All checks passed |
| `uv run mypy` | no issues in 132 source files |
| `uv build && uv run python scripts/validate_package.py` | wheel + sdist 0.2.0, VALIDATION OK |
| `uv run python scripts/smoke_hermes_plugin.py --testbed …` | SMOKE OK, 75 checks |
| `git diff --check` | clean |

Concurrency (`tests/test_controls_concurrency.py`): sixteen simultaneous flushes are one flush, eight claimants are one claim, eight sync requests are one scheduled pass, four *processes* asking for a flush produce one request, a retry landing inside a batch claim never gives one turn to two batches, a `/cb sync` typed between a real pass's fetch and its push produces no second push, and no control waits for the profile write lock.

Privacy (`tests/test_controls_privacy.py`): a credential in a captured turn, one in a committed document, one typed into `remember`, a remote URL with a token, a customer's email and phone, a prompt marker and tool chatter — then every command on both surfaces, and a grep of stdout, stderr, the text `/cb` posts, the JSON a script parses, every DEBUG log record, and the raw bytes of both databases.

## Manifest and metadata

The manifest description no longer claims "Nothing is ever applied or committed", which stopped being true in PR #5 and PR #7. Version is `0.2.0` in the manifest, the package and `pyproject.toml`. The package validator now checks the five new modules, `__main__.py`, and that the wheel actually declares the console script.

## Not in this PR, by design

No model-facing tool, no `hermes context …` namespace, no control that acts inside a turn, no configuration written by a command, no repository repair, no conflict resolution, no remote provisioning, no new opt-in — and no release hardening (PR #9).

## Safety

Every test and the smoke run used a throwaway `HERMES_HOME`, a fixture OKF repository under `tmp_path` and a bare "remote" that is a directory. No live Hermes profile was written to, installed into or started; no real remote was contacted; no canary was run; the pinned testbed is clean.

body:
## What and why

Dogfooding the freshly deployed gateway audio endpoints in the Trace Explorer surfaced three defects (customer report: only transcription traces visible, empty input and output on them, and "gpt-5-mini" rendered as "5-mini").

1. **Every successful TTS span was silently eaten.** The zero-cost probe suppression in the customer trace bridge (built for claude-code's system-reminder pings: no completion tokens, no cost, no extracted output) structurally matches every speech span, every duration-priced STT span (scribe reports seconds, not tokens), and embeddings. The heuristic is now gated to chat-shaped request types, the only shape probes actually have.
2. **Audio traces had empty input and output.** Speech spans now carry the synthesized text as the input message; transcription spans carry the transcript as the output message.
3. **Model-name magic in the trace UI.** A hardcoded abbreviation table shortened ids ("gpt-5-mini" to "5-mini", "gpt-4o" to "4o"), and a follow-up rule stripped Anthropic's `[1m]` context-variant suffix. Both are gone: model ids render exactly as reported. The `[1m]` marker stays visible on purpose, it says which context tier served the request and Anthropic already prices long context differently. With no transforms left, `abbreviateModel` was the identity function, so it is deleted and every surface renders the raw id.

## Proof

Live local stack (app + gateway + real keys), spans read back from ClickHouse after the fix:

```
SpanName: gen_ai.speech
input:    [{"role":"user","content":"The gateway now traces speech calls end to end."}]

SpanName: gen_ai.transcription
output:   [{"role":"assistant","content":"The gateway now traces speech calls end-to-end."}]
```

Before the fix the same probe produced only the transcription row; the speech span never reached the wire.

## Tests

- `TestEmitter_SpeechSpanIsNotSuppressedAsProbe` (bound to the audio spec's TTS-trace scenario) proves a zero-token, zero-cost speech span reaches the OTLP wire; `TestEmitter_ZeroChatProbeStaysSuppressed` proves the probe suppression still works for its actual target.
- Extraction tests for the new speech-input and transcription-output message shapes.
- `TestSpeechDispatchEmitsCustomerSpan` pins the pipeline plumbing for speech dispatches.
- `abbreviateModel` tests rewritten for the as-is contract.

## Deployment Impact

- Gateway service redeploy picks up the span fixes; app deploy picks up the UI change. No schema or config changes.
- Behavior change: previously hidden spans (audio, embeddings with zero completion tokens) become visible, which is the point; claude-code probe suppression is unchanged.

author: gustavovalverde
body:
The explorer materialized views have no writer. The driver that builds them reads through the legacy `PrimaryChainStore`, and the shipped `zinder-ingest` binary stopped opening one, so nothing in the release composition can populate the store `zinder-explorer` serves. This ports the write path onto canonical storage and wires it into the ingest runtime.

Canonical storage already holds everything required. No new column family, no schema bump, no rebuild of deployed stores.

## What changes

- **Canonical reads**: a point read for one retained block's facts on the canonical secondary, plus a conversion from a retained canonical transition into a dispatchable chain event. Heights outside the admitted range return `None`; a missing row inside it is a sequence error, because READY admission proves contiguity.
- **Derived hydration**: final note commitment roots are computed by seeding a commitment-tree accumulator from the nearest tree-state checkpoint and appending persisted compact-block commitments. The roots column family is empty on every wallet-workload store, so reading it would return an empty view forever. Transparent spends resolve through the transaction location index to the producing block's replay row.
- **Ingest owns the plane**: the process opens one in-process canonical secondary at `<storage.path>.materialized-view-secondary` and writes the view store nested under the canonical path. The writer handle never serves these reads, so its cross-block read counters stay at zero.
- **Interrupted builds resume**: the driver gap-fills unmaterialized heights after every event drain instead of seeding once, so a crash mid-build resumes where it stopped rather than stranding every height above the last page.
- **Expired cursors recover**: an expired canonical event cursor triggers a bounded synthetic reorg over the reorg window. It previously warned and retried forever.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Breaking. A store built with `ingest.run_overrides.checkpoint_height` is refused for materialized-view work rather than serving under-reported rows: cumulative address views resolve spends against the producing block, so history starting above block 1 is silently wrong. The `[storage.materialized_views]` RocksDB budget section now also applies to `zinder-ingest`.

## Fails closed, not quiet

Three failure modes here produce a plausible but empty or partial view rather than an error, so each is a typed failure instead: a commitment-tree seeding failure, an unresolved non-coinbase prevout, and an unreadable persisted cursor. The consumers treat absence as "no spend" and `None` roots as "nothing to index", so silence would have been indistinguishable from correctness.

## Removed

The ranking bootstrap depends on a settled address-balance snapshot that canonical storage does not have, and the materialized-view status reader was a trait with one implementation and no callers. Both are deleted, along with the benchmark materialized-view arm, which is built end to end on the legacy store.

## Coverage note for review

`services/zinder-explorer/tests/live/fee_summary_federation.rs` is deleted rather than ported. It seeded its view store by running the legacy driver over a legacy bulk-catchup store across a 50-block checkpointed range, which the new genesis-completeness gate refuses by design. Restoring that coverage belongs with the explorer read-plane port. The explorer integration bootstrap keeps its reorg-incident coverage by dispatching retained event envelopes directly into the consumer.

## Follow-ups this does not do

Explorer read-plane migration off the legacy `SecondaryChainStore`, ranking bootstrap redesign, and the mempool-event-counts writer.

body:
Tem Script? | Novas Env Vars
-- | --
Não | Não

> :warning: **NOTA**
> - `tempest openapi-errors --fix` **edita código-fonte do projeto do usuário**. Só grava com árvore git limpa (`git status --porcelain` vazio) — assim `git diff` é a revisão e `git checkout -- .` é o desfazer. Com mudança pendente sai 1 sem escrever nada.
> - `--dry-run` é somente leitura: imprime o diff unificado e roda em árvore suja.
> - O fixer **só acrescenta**. Findings `unreachable` nunca são removidos.
> - Sem migration, sem env var, sem dependência nova.

## Problema

A v0.160.0 entregou o `tempest openapi-errors --check`: ele percorre `router -> controller -> service -> repository` com `ast` e reporta, por rota, as `AppException` alcançáveis que a rota não declarou (`undocumented`) e as declaradas que o fluxo não alcança (`unreachable`).

O comando parava aí. Num projeto que já existe ele aponta dezenas de rotas, e fechar cada uma é trabalho puramente mecânico: abrir o arquivo, escrever `responses=error_responses(...)` no decorator, importar o helper, importar cada classe de exception. O analisador já sabe exatamente o que escrever e em qual linha — deixar isso para a mão é o tipo de tarefa em que se erra o import, se esquece uma rota do meio da lista, e o `--check` continua vermelho.

Havia ainda um risco de adoção: o gate de CI é fácil de ligar num projeto novo e desanimador num projeto legado, porque o custo inicial de sincronizar cai todo de uma vez.

## Solução

### A. `--fix` — escrever as declarações que faltam

`tempest openapi-errors --fix` grava o que o `--check` apontava.

Rota que não declara nada ganha o parâmetro e os imports:

```diff
+from tempest_fastapi_sdk import error_responses
+
+from src.core.exceptions import CandidateAlreadyExistsException, ServiceFullException

-@router.post("/{service_id}/candidates", status_code=201)
+@router.post(
+    "/{service_id}/candidates",
+    status_code=201,
+    responses=error_responses(
+        CandidateAlreadyExistsException, ServiceFullException
+    ),
+)
```

Rota que já declara parte tem a declaração **estendida**, com a ordem original preservada:

```diff
-    responses=error_responses(ServiceNotFoundException),
+    responses=error_responses(ServiceNotFoundException, ServiceFullException),
```

Um `@raises(...)` existente também é estendido no lugar. Já a rota que não declara nada sempre recebe `error_responses`, nunca `@raises`: `@raises` só é lido pelo `TempestAPIRouter`, então injetá-lo num projeto de `APIRouter` puro produziria um decorator que não faz nada — o pior resultado possível para uma ferramenta que existe para fechar um buraco de documentação. Um `@raises` já presente prova que o projeto optou por esse estilo, e aí ele é respeitado.

### B. As três propriedades que tornam a reescrita automática defensável

**Edições ancoradas na AST.** Cada inserção é posicionada no parêntese de fechamento de um nó de call (`RouteInfo` agora carrega `decorator_end` / `error_responses_end` / `raises_end`), nunca numa regex. Nada depende de como o decorator está formatado, e o resto do arquivo — comentários, layout — não é tocado.

**Só acrescenta.** Findings `unreachable` são deliberadamente ignorados. Alcançabilidade resolve por nome de chamada e não enxerga raise dinâmico, então apagar uma declaração baseado nela removeria declaração correta. Curadoria de lista inflada continua manual, e o relatório continua mostrando esses casos.

**Árvore git limpa obrigatória para gravar.** Com a árvore limpa, `git diff` é a revisão e `git checkout` é o desfazer — a rede de segurança real de uma ferramenta que edita código que o usuário escreveu. Árvore suja sai 1 com a instrução. `--dry-run` é somente leitura e roda em qualquer estado.

### C. Preview idêntico à gravação

O splice cru é uma linha só, então um decorator já quebrado em linhas sairia longo demais e o import novo cairia fora da ordem. As duas coisas são resolvidas por `normalize()` — `ruff check --select I --fix` + `ruff format` — usado pelos **dois** caminhos. Um preview diferente do que a gravação produz é pior que preview nenhum.

### D. Import que não resolve não é escrito

O import é derivado do arquivo que define a classe (`exception_locations()`). Nome definido em mais de um arquivo, ou fora da raiz varrida, é ambíguo — escrever o import errado quebraria a aplicação. Nesse caso a rota é pulada e o nome sai listado como `unresolved` para ser declarado à mão.

author: brunoalr
body:
## Why

Drawing a buffer indexes it as `(y * step + x) * channels`, and nothing on that path checks the result against the memory it was given. A buffer that describes more pixels than it carries therefore reads past the end of its allocation while drawing pixel values.

`configure()` already refused a buffer that claims *too much* memory. This bounds the other side: too little for the picture it describes.

## Where the check belongs

At the render layer, because that is the one every source funnels through — messages from the debugger, and buffers loaded from a file. Placing it here means a new source cannot bypass it.

To be clear about what it is worth today: the message paths already validate geometry against the payload, and the `.npy` loader already refuses a file whose data section disagrees with its declared dimensions. **No producer shipping today can reach this guard.** It is defence in depth, not a fix for a reachable hole.

## Two details that are easy to get wrong

**An element is not always the size its type says.** A float64 buffer is narrowed to float32 on the way in while keeping its float64 tag, and the renderer reads it back as float. Sizing one at eight bytes per element would reject every valid float64 buffer by a factor of two.

**The final row needs only `width` pixels**, not the full row stride, so a buffer that trims its trailing padding is still accepted. The comparison divides rather than multiplies, because the equivalent product overflows for hostile geometry.

## Testing

The rule is a header free of GL types, so it is unit tested directly: exact fits, one byte short, trimmed final rows, nonsense geometry, overflow, and the float64 sizing. All 13 fixtures in `testbench/realtypes.cpp` were also plotted in a live debug session — none is refused, including the strided Eigen map whose final row is trimmed.

body:
## Summary

Adds `npx sliccy --install-cli` (plus optional `--install-dir <dir>`) — a one-shot installer that downloads the released Go `slicc` follower binary (`packages/slicc-cli`) for the current platform into `~/.slicc/bin` and exits without booting the server.

## Why

The `slicc` follower CLI ships as bare signed binaries on GitHub releases, but there has been no installation story beyond manually hunting through release assets. `npx sliccy --install-cli` gives anyone with Node a one-liner. Part of a series with the upcoming `sliccy.ai/install-cli` curl|sh installer and a `slicc update` self-update command.

## Approach / Implementation notes

- `runtime-flags.ts` gains `installCli` (bare flag) and `installDir` (both `--install-dir=<dir>` and `--install-dir <dir>` forms). Dispatch in `index.ts` sits right after the `--version` block, before FileLogger/server side effects.
- New `src/install-cli.ts` owns everything and is fully injectable (`fetchImpl`, platform/arch, env, log sinks) for tests.
- **Sparse releases**: CLI binaries only attach to releases where `packages/slicc-cli` changed (`release-native.mjs` gating), so the newest release may not carry them. The installer scans releases newest→oldest (per_page=30, page cap 5) for the first one with this platform's `slicc-<os>-<arch>[.exe]` asset — the same approach as the worker's `/download/slicc.dmg` route.
- Download goes to a staging file in the target dir, `chmod 0755`, then an atomic rename; the staging file is removed on every failure path.
- Platform map mirrors the `packages/slicc-cli/Makefile` dist matrix: darwin/linux/windows × amd64/arm64.

## Cross-cutting impact

- **Floats exercised**: CLI only — the flag is a new early-exit path in node-server's entrypoint; no server, extension, Electron, or worker code paths change.
- No persisted-state changes beyond writing the requested binary; `~/.slicc/bin` follows the existing `~/.slicc` convention (secrets, logs, cloud-sessions).
- No new dependencies; undici `fetch` follows the GitHub asset redirect natively.

author: tamnd
body:
A module may define a module-level `__getattr__(name)` that is consulted for any
name missing from its namespace (PEP 562). unagi did not support it, so a
`from typing import Match` failed with `cannot import name 'Match' from 'typing'`
and `typing.ContextManager`, `typing.Pattern` and the rest of typing's lazily
built names were unreachable.

Changes:

- `pkg/objects/module.go` moduleLoadAttr consults a module-level `__getattr__`
  for a name absent from the namespace, skipping the lookup for `__getattr__`
  itself and letting an AttributeError the hook raises surface unchanged.
- `pkg/runtime/modules.go` ImportFrom consults the same hook so
  `from module import name` resolves a lazily served name, falling through to
  the ordinary ImportError wording when the hook declines with AttributeError.
- `pkg/objects/class.go` a module-qualified builtin type value now answers
  `__module__` with the part before the last dot (re.Match -> 're'), a bare
  type name with builtins. typing._alias reads `re.Match.__module__` when it
  builds the Match and Pattern aliases.

importlib.metadata, which imports typing.Match, now imports fully.

Tests: pkg/objects unit tests for the hook (served name, declined name, bound
name wins, __module__ of a qualified and a bare type), plus conformance fixture
2221_module_getattr_pep562 (a custom lazy module and the real typing.Match/
Pattern/ContextManager path). Full local gate green (cross-platform build,
pkg/runtime, pkg/objects, pkg/lower).

author: bartekus
body:
Two things that arrived together, because the second found the first.

## 1. The 009 fail-loud test ran, and passed

Section 5's oldest open acceptance item ("remove a required key, watch the crash loop, restore it") ran against the live control plane on 2026-07-25, deliberately, once.

`GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET` was removed from the live pod Secret and the pod replaced. The same key the failed 2026-07-21 run used, so the results are directly comparable:

```
[required-env] GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET is empty or unset
[required-env] refusing to start; missing: GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET
```

exit code 1, `CrashLoopBackOff` within 33 seconds, edge serving 503. In 2026-07-21 the identical removal produced a **healthy pod and a silent 401**. The section 4.2 wrapper does exactly what it was built to do.

The method is recorded as carefully as the result, because the restore path is the reusable part: suspend the `secrets` Flux Kustomization so reconciliation cannot race the test, JSON-patch the key out, replace the pod by deleting it (never `rollout restart` on a Flux-managed Deployment), then **resume Flux so the restore comes from git rather than from anything typed by hand**. The restored value was byte-compared against the pre-test value before the local copy was destroyed. Deliberate downtime: about three minutes.

## 2. The recovery restart exposed a real defect

The recovery boot crash-looped three times on its own, on a pod replacement with nothing else wrong with it:

```
thread 'tokio-rt-worker' panicked at hiqlite-wal-0.14.0/src/log_store.rs:47:21:
LockFile /data/rauthy/db/logs is locked and in use by another process
```

`docker/entrypoint.sh` is PID 1 and had **no signal handler**. The runtime signals PID 1 and nothing else, so on every container stop the shell died alone and rauthy was SIGKILLed at the end of the grace period, never releasing its hiqlite WAL and state-machine locks. Every boot after every restart began unclean (three `LockFile ... exists already` warnings, present on the successful boot too), and intermittently a stale lock read as live aborts rauthy, which die-together turns into a crash loop.

Same failure shape as the seventeen-hour outage in §4.6 item 5, reached from an ordinary `kubectl delete pod`.

**The fix**: a handler forwarding SIGTERM/SIGINT to both children and waiting for them before exiting 0, armed right after `RAUTHY_PID` is assigned so a stop during the rauthy health wait is covered.

**The test**: `docker/entrypoint.test.ts`, the first test in this repo over `docker/`. It covers the *shipped* function rather than a copy: the `shutdown()` body is lifted out of `entrypoint.sh` by text and run against stub children, so editing the real function breaks the test. Verified in the other direction by hand: with the trap removed the harness exits 143 and neither child is signalled at all.

The same hunk lands upstream in enrahitu (its spec 007, statecrafting/enrahitu#31), so spec 002 records it as **convergent, not a fifth divergence** — a chassis entrypoint fix does not reach a stamped app through a pin, only through the next sync.

## 3. Diagnosed and deliberately not fixed

The recurring `Error creating backup: ... output file already exists` is **not a failing backup**. Backups are healthy: four consecutive daily files, no gaps. The errors are raft log replay: on boot hiqlite re-applies past `Backup` entries with their original timestamps, and the timestamp is the filename, so `VACUUM main INTO` hits a file that already exists. Four errors, matching the four retained files, all within 200ms of startup. Upstream carries the literal `TODO include a TS in the req to skip backups if they are replayed after a restart`.

This corrects my earlier "every few minutes" reading: it is once per boot, once per retained backup, and the E2E made it look periodic only because the pod was restarting more than expected (which finding 1 now explains). Not ours to fix: rauthy pins `hiqlite` from crates.io with its `[patch.crates-io]` block commented out, so the local fork is not in this image's dependency path. Worth an upstream issue; the one real cost is that it scales with `HQL_BACKUP_KEEP_DAYS` (30 here), so it will eventually bury a genuine backup failure.

## Verification

Full suite 174 passed (libsql + Postgres arms), `tsc --noEmit` clean, `spec-spine lint` 0/0/0, `couple` OK across 4 paths.

## Residual

The deployed image predates this handler. Closing finding 1 in production needs one image rebuild and digest re-pin, deliberately not improvised on the same night as the test.

body:
Adds real progress feedback to a running check, and fixes two deeper causes that local testing exposed. Also corrects a design inconsistency in the trust signals. **Observability only — no verdict, score, or lifecycle state is read or changed.**

## The reported problem
Starting a check gave no feedback: the bar sat frozen and you couldn't tell whether extraction or analysis was happening.

## Three causes, not one
| # | Cause | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | The analysis phase emitted **no events** until it finished (`check_result` fires in one burst after the loop) | bar showed a fetch-only count |
| 2 | **Events were never committed mid-run.** `_emit()` only `session.add()`s; the live path committed once at the very end | a 7-minute run had exactly **1 visible event** — the old bar could never have moved either |
| 3 | **The event loop was blocked.** The checker, URL ranker and cluster labeler are synchronous LLM calls awaited directly in async code | **`/health` itself timed out at 8s** during a run — the whole API was frozen, so nothing could poll |

## The fix
- Emit `node_started(check)`, `material_checked` per material, `node_started(cluster)`.
- **Commit** progress events so they're visible mid-run (safe: session factory already uses `expire_on_commit=False`).
- Dispatch the three blocking calls via `asyncio.to_thread`. **Verified: the API answered every poll through a full live run.**
- Server-derived progress (`derive_progress`, 12 unit tests) on `GET /products/{id}` for **active runs only**.
- Card shows phase → counter → percent → `~N min left`, with "estimating time…" until the estimate is trustworthy.
- Dropped the now-redundant per-run events poll.

## Also: trust signal consistency
The verifier row showed *alongside* measured accuracy, but the reliability badge *replaced* it — so it was invisible on certified rules. They answer different questions (per-rule historical vs per-flag structural), so both now show. Verified locally: reliability present on 26/26 flags.

body:
## Summary

- **Retrieval now filters by the active embedding profile, and refuses partial coverage.** Vectors from every provider share 1,536 dimensions, so Postgres computes a cosine distance between a Gemini query vector and a deterministic stored vector without complaint — mathematically valid, semantically meaningless, and visible only as plausible false matches. `material_chunks.embedding_model` is now a bound predicate in the eligible-chunk CTE, and a profile-coverage check runs *before* the query is embedded so a course with no compatible vectors never spends provider quota. **Strict course readiness**: one incompletely embedded candidate material blocks grounded retrieval for that whole course.
- **The embedding port is redesigned around asymmetric providers.** `embedBatch(texts)` cannot express which side of an asymmetric model it is embedding, and every live model targeted here prefixes queries and documents differently. It becomes `embedQuery` + `embedDocuments`, with `EmbeddingDocument` carrying a title. Titles are plumbed **now** rather than later: a live adapter reports a fixed document profile, so folding titles in afterwards would change the vector space while `embedding_model` stayed identical.
- **`queryProtocol` is versioned separately from `model`.** Both retrieval task types share one document format, so folding them together would make a query-task experiment cost a corpus-wide re-embed. It is **diagnostic only** — `message_retrievals` has no column for it, so it reaches structured logs and metrics and nowhere else. This is not provenance.
- **Shared upstream primitives extracted to `common/`.** The ITI gateway URL policy is an SSRF boundary and `readBoundedResponseBody` encodes a socket-leak fix; neither may exist in two copies that can drift. `waitForRetry` and `readBoundedResponseBody` now take the caller's error factory, and the Gemini quota guard takes a **required** namespace — a default would let an embedding ingest silently inherit the interactive chat budget. Completion keeps its vocabulary through thin shims, pinned by a digest regression **and** a Redis-state compatibility test.
- **A guarded Gemini embedding provider.** `gemini-embedding-2` at 1,536 dimensions, pinned in code because the model *is* part of the persisted document profile. Two SDK traps are handled structurally: `taskType` is unsupported and made unnameable via `Pick`; a bare `string[]` as `contents` makes the SDK return one aggregated vector, so each input is sent as its own `Content` and a one-embedding response to a multi-input request is rejected.
- **Quota is atomic and estimate-only.** Request and estimated input units are reserved in one Redis operation before the upstream call, so an exhausted budget makes zero calls to Google. The estimate is never reconciled — the pinned SDK's Developer-API conversion discards `usageMetadata` entirely, asserted in a contract test so an SDK upgrade fails loudly. The caps are **local admission control informed by published limits**, not a reproduction of Google's enforcement; provider-side `429`s remain authoritative.
- **A runnable, resumable migration** — `npm run embedding:migrate -- <target>`. Resumption is driven by database state, not a cursor: a cursor would advance past a material that failed while a later one succeeded and skip it permanently. The target is an explicit argument validated independently of `EMBEDDING_PROVIDER`, because the point is to migrate *before* switching. It exits non-zero unless the whole corpus is covered, which is what stops a provider switch off a partially successful run.
- **Also included:** a shared batching primitive with deterministic lowest-index failure selection (under concurrency the highest-index task can fail first in wall-clock time, so "first rejection wins" would report a worker chosen by scheduling), three separate embedding deadlines, and the documented maintenance-mode procedure for switching providers.

### Deliberately not included: the ITI Cohere embedding adapter

`aws-bedrock` stays out of the `EMBEDDING_PROVIDER` enum. Public AWS docs establish the model's contract, but every gateway-specific fact about `/student/embed` — the route, the request body, the response envelope, whether the account is approved for `us.cohere.embed-v4:0`, and whether the gateway preserves the 1,536-dimensional default — is unverified, and no ITI credential is present locally to probe with. Implementing against an invented envelope would let an error response resemble a valid shape and produce tests proving compatibility with a payload nobody has observed. The unblocking probe is specified in `docs/aws-bedrock-iti-gateway-research.md`.

The Gemini query-task comparison (`search result` vs `question answering`) is likewise recorded as outstanding in `docs/gemini-embedding-task-selection.md`; `search result` is the initial candidate, not a measured winner.

## Validation

- [x] `npm run check` — 50 suites, 846 tests, lint `--max-warnings=0`, typecheck, build
- [x] If acceptance-test behavior changed: `npm run infra:up`, `npm run db:migrate:deploy`, and `npm run test:e2e` (followed by `npm run infra:down`) — 24 suites, 293 tests
- [x] `npm run test:e2e:gate-2 --workspace server` — the tightest similarity-sensitive check; the four gate-2 fixture vectors are unchanged

## Scope Check

- [x] No auth, RBAC, RAG, embeddings, AI provider code, role shells, app Dockerfiles, or production deployment config were added unless this PR is explicitly scoped for that work. — **This PR is explicitly scoped for embeddings and AI provider code.**
- [x] `.env.example` files were updated for any new required variables. — both `.env.example` and `server/.env.example`, plus `docker-compose.yml`.

## Activation

Gemini embedding is refused when `NODE_ENV=production` and requires `GEMINI_EMBEDDING_DEMO_ACKNOWLEDGED=true` — Morshid's free-tier data-governance policy, not an API constraint. Its key must be distinct from `GEMINI_API_KEY` **and** live under a separate Google Cloud project, since Gemini limits are per project; the schema can only prove the keys differ.

Before switching `EMBEDDING_PROVIDER`, run the maintenance-mode migration to complete active-profile coverage (`server/README.md`). Existing deterministic rows **must** be replaced before a live provider is activated — strict readiness will otherwise block every course.

## Why

PR #53 left one named gap: "Keep as relevant" still 404'd in the preview harness, because a rescue runs the whole scanner pipeline before its RPC. This PR closes it. Test-harness and E2E only — no `src/` change, no baseline regenerated, no migration.

## What the shim gained

The minimum surface `rescueRejectedCandidate` actually calls, written against `src/lib/automation/run.ts`:

- **POST `automation_runs`** (insert returning id) and **PATCH** — `createRunLedger` / `finalizeRunLedgerSafely`
- **POST `source_signals`** — `upsertSignal`'s first-observation branch, with the force-hidden cluster trigger applied on insert; the reobserve branch rides the pre-existing PATCH handler
- **POST `signal_observation_events`** — the rescue-retry ledger (reachable only from production-shaped preview seeds, stated in the comment)
- **POST `issue_clusters`** — `createCluster`, for a rescue that routes nowhere
- **PATCH `automation_rejected_candidates`** — the `rescued_at` mark that takes a kept candidate off the desk
- **filterRows**: `external_id_hash=eq`, `semantic_fingerprint=eq`, `source=neq`, `slug=eq`, `slug=not.like`, and generic `not.is.null` — with SQL's three-valued NULL semantics on the negations

Two of those filters are load-bearing, not cosmetic: without `slug=eq`, `findAutoClusterBySlug` returned `clusters[0]` — the public FPS cluster — so a rescue would have silently attached its signal to the headline public issue. Without `not.is.null`, `findExistingSignalCluster` routed by whatever row came first.

The extraction step needs no stub: without `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` the app itself falls back to deterministic extraction before any network call (`extract.ts:311`).

## What the test proves

One new test submits the real **Keep as relevant** form on `/scanner`: the whole pipeline runs server-side — run ledger, deterministic extraction, cluster routing, signal insert, stats refresh, decision RPC, rescued_at — and any missing surface fails the POST loudly. Then the candidate is gone from the desk, the KEEP lesson is visible, and **Undo does not bring the candidate back** — that last assertion is the proof `rescued_at` landed (the desk filter alone would also hide a decision-only candidate), and it exercises the undo RPC's rescued-skip branch.

## Fixture isolation, the honest version

A rescue has no UI control that fully reverses it, and rendering `/scanner` after the write repopulates two `PUBLIC_DASHBOARD_TAG` cache entries with post-rescue rows — the locked-vocabulary hero numbers. The fixture reset cannot evict those. So the test cleans up after itself: mid-test reset, then one idempotent patch-override write (same version) that makes the app revalidate every public tag against the restored rows.

Proven by execution, not argument: with a persistent harness server, the rescue test ran **alone**, then both screenshot projects ran against that same server's caches — 31 passed, 5 pre-existing viewport skips, zero baseline drift.

## Review

One fresh-context adversarial review (Opus 5, high effort) ran before this draft. Fixed from it: the false cache-isolation comment and the order-dependence it hid (P2), a duplicate PATCH handler (P2), the undo-proves-rescued_at gap (P3), NULL semantics on `neq`/`not.like` (P3), the skipped force-hidden trigger on signal insert (P3), and the header now names the two remaining gaps — the live scan trigger and the unenforced `issue_clusters` slug unique index (23505 recovery has no harness coverage; unreachable from a clean fixture).

Full Playwright 36 passed / 5 pre-existing skips (write project first, all baselines intact), N=0 E2E, ESLint, `tsc --noEmit`, 929 unit tests, `git diff --check` — all fresh on the final tree. Production build green on this branch; diff is test-only.

author: gajesh2007
body:
Found by the paged-vs-contiguous differential oracle on its **first run** — a latent process abort in the backend we ship **today**, not in the one we are migrating to.

`CBv2AttentionV1` passes `sinks` straight to `scaledDotProductAttention` without matching the query dtype. fp16 queries with fp32 sinks reach `FatalError: Type of sinks must promote to output type float16` — a daemon abort, so every co-resident model's in-flight requests are lost, with no telemetry.

Paged returns a correct answer on identical inputs: `PagedLayerCache` already coerces, and documents why in an 18-line comment. The paged author defended the trap; the contiguous one did not.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Before
    A1[fp16 queries + fp32 sinks] --> B1[CBv2AttentionV1]
    B1 --> C1[scaledDotProductAttention]
    C1 --> D1[FatalError: sinks must promote]
    D1 --> E1[daemon abort - all slots lose in-flight work]
  end
  subgraph After
    A2[fp16 queries + fp32 sinks] --> B2[CBv2AttentionV1]
    B2 --> F2[sinks.asType queries.dtype]
    F2 --> C2[scaledDotProductAttention]
    C2 --> E2[correct output, matches paged]
  end
```

Every contiguous route traced to its terminal rather than pattern-matched: the two `composedAttention` sites are deliberately exempt because they cast internally. Divergence can only arise on the dtype path, never rounding — the generated sinks carry bit-identical values that widen fp16 to fp32.

**Verified:** `CBv2AttentionSinkDtypeTests`; the differential oracle now agrees across both backends on this shape.

author: gajesh2007
body:
Stacks on #86 (seam contract), which declares `CBv2PagedSpeculation`, `CBv2PagedSpeculativeRow` and `CBv2MTPRectangularSerializing`.

Four coupled changes in one PR because they were developed against each other — three are only correct once the other two land, so splitting further produces links that do not compile.

**1. The ring was sized from the window alone.** A windowed row's earliest live query must still see its full window while the chunk it is attending is already resident, so the real attendable range is `window - 1 + maxPrefillChunk`. The first shrink to 65 pages aborted **ordinary** windowed prefill — no speculation involved.

**2. Paged prefill never sub-blocked its queries.** Contiguous has blocked at q=128 since #85. Migrating without this would have *regressed* prefill memory 4x.

**3. Gather before the write**, so the ring is only ever asked for `window-1` tokens.

**4. A speculative round is a transaction**, with orphan pages drained on teardown.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph Before
    R1["ring = ceil(window/pageSize) + headroom — sized from the window alone"]
    P1["prefillAttend: ONE SDPA over the full rectangle — [1,8,512,1535] = 2.04 GB at 124k"]
    W1["row.write THEN gather — ring must hold window-1+chunk"]
    S1["speculative write with ad-hoc rollback"]
  end
  subgraph After
    R2["ring = ceil((window-1+chunk)/ps) + ceil(span/ps) — DERIVED, pinned from both sides"]
    P2["blocked loop with its own .array mask — 4 x [1,8,128,1151], gather hoisted"]
    W2["gather(pre-write history) ++ chunk THEN row.write"]
    S2["begin/commit/rollback as a transaction — orphan pages drained on teardown"]
  end
```

Three traps a naive port hits, all avoided:

- paged must **not** call the private `attendQueryBlocks` — its `maskMode` returns symbolic `.causal`, which violates this file's always-`.array` contract;
- the gather stays **hoisted** — per-block gathering is a 3x pessimisation on sliding layers (spans overlap by `window-1`) and 4x on full;
- `qpos`/`kpos` are built once per chunk and sliced — rebuilding them per block regresses host `arange` work 4x.

gemma-4 stays at 97 pages. The size is unchanged; what changed is that it is now **derived** from the quantity it must cover instead of coinciding with it, and pinned from both sides rather than against a literal that moves.

The real memory win additionally needs a **row-level** answer, because direct writers (`PagedSequenceKV.write` then `attendableViews`) cannot re-gather post-write — their bound is `ringTokens - window + 1`, not `maxPrefillChunk`. Scheduled separately; the constraint is documented in the tree so nobody picks it up expecting a one-liner.

Also lands the paged-vs-contiguous differential oracle, which found two real defects on its first run and is proven non-vacuous by perturbing the paged arm until it goes red.

**Verified:** 228 tests / 35 suites; query-blocking suites pass with blocking both on and off.

author: richmondjw
body:
Reported from a phone: on `/me/trip/` the **Move** button sat half off-screen and **Remove** was cut off entirely.

## Root cause

`.trip-list` and `.trip-day__list` are both `display: grid`. Grid items default to `min-width: auto`, so neither the day group nor the stop row would shrink below its own content width.

| element | width | right edge | container right edge |
|---|---|---|---|
| `.trip-list` | 327 | 351 | 351 |
| `.trip-day` | **371** | **395** | 351 |
| `.trip-stop` | **371** | **395** | 351 |
| `.trip-stop__actions` | 140 | **382** | 351 |

44px past its own parent at a 375px viewport. The body sets `overflow-x: hidden`, so it clipped rather than scrolled, which is why Remove was not merely off-screen but **untappable**.

Adding `min-width: 0` stops the overflow but is not on its own a fix: the row then honours the container by crushing the title instead, down to ~75px and a five-line wrap. The 64px media tile, the title and two 48px targets genuinely do not fit on one line at phone widths.

So below `32.49em` the actions take their own right-aligned row. The media tile and title stay side by side above it, which keeps the desktop rhythm rather than stacking everything.

## Choosing the breakpoint

Not the site's usual `35.94em` phone breakpoint. The threshold was picked from where the title stops having room:

| viewport | title width, single row | title lines |
|---|---|---|
| 375 | 75 | 5 |
| 480 | 178 | 3 |
| **520** | **220** | 2 |
| 600 | 298 | 2 |

520px (`32.49em`) is where a two-line title fits, so that is where the wrap ends. Worth flagging as a judgement call: matching `35.94em` for consistency is a one-value change.

## Verification

Measured across eight widths, checking every element against the viewport:

| width | row / container | actions right edge | overflowing elements |
|---|---|---|---|
| 320 | 272 / 272 | 283 (in) | 0 |
| 375 | 327 / 327 | 338 (in) | 0 |
| 390 | 342 / 342 | 353 (in) | 0 |
| 414 | 366 / 366 | 377 (in) | 0 |
| 480 | 432 / 432 | 443 (in) | 0 |
| 600 | 552 / 552 | 563 (in) | 0 |
| 768 | 720 / 720 | 731 (in) | 0 |
| 1440 | 852 / 852 | 1133 (in) | 0 |

Both 48px targets fully visible at every width, and `scrollWidth === clientWidth` throughout.

600px and above are unchanged: the single-row layout measures identically child by child, since the two `min-width: 0` additions are non-binding once the content fits. Desktop screenshot confirms no visual change.

Card height at 375 also drops **228px to 152px**, the title now getting 225px and two lines instead of 75px and five.

author: moveeeax
body:
Cloud Spanner holds data, so this change is focused on destruction semantics
and on the data-protection controls the module did not expose at all.

## What was actually wrong

**Instance sizing (real bug).** `num_nodes` defaulted to `1` and
`processing_units` was not exposed at all, so the module could only ever
provision whole nodes. 1 node == 1000 processing units, meaning the smallest
instance this module could build was roughly **10x the cost** of the smallest
instance Spanner offers (100 PU). `processing_units` is now a first-class input.

**Mutual exclusivity was unenforced.** `num_nodes` and `processing_units` are
mutually exclusive in the provider. Setting both now fails at *plan* time via a
resource precondition instead of at apply time via a provider error. (It has to
be a precondition rather than a `variable "..." { validation }` because
cross-variable validation needs Terraform >= 1.9 and this module supports >= 1.5.)
`processing_units` granularity is validated too: multiple of 100 below 1000,
multiple of 1000 at or above.

**No instance-level destroy protection existed.** `google_spanner_instance` has
no `deletion_protection` field in google provider >= 5.0 (`deletion_policy` was
only added in a later major, so it is not usable at this module's declared
floor). The control that *does* work at >= 5.0 is
`google_spanner_database.enable_drop_protection`, which is enforced by the
Spanner API rather than by Terraform state: it blocks drops made outside
Terraform **and** blocks deletion of the parent instance. It is now exposed per
database.

**PITR and CMEK were not exposed.** `version_retention_period` (1h..7d) and
`encryption_config.kms_key_name` are now inputs, with plan-time format
validation so typos like `"7days"` or a bare key name fail before apply.
`database_dialect` is exposed and validated as well.

**The example taught callers to switch the guard off.** `examples/basic` set
`deletion_protection = false`. It now leaves the guard on, uses 100 processing
units, and documents the deliberate two-step teardown.

**New: plan-time warning for unprotected databases.** A `check` block warns when
a database has both `deletion_protection` and `enable_drop_protection` disabled,
because Spanner keeps no backups by default and a destroy at that point is
unrecoverable.

## What was already fine (checked, left alone)

- `deletion_protection` already defaulted to `true` for databases, matching the
  provider default. The module was **not** weakening it. Unchanged, and now
  pinned by a test.
- The module declares **no IAM resources at all**, so there is no authoritative
  `google_spanner_database_iam_binding` / `_policy` used where `_member` was
  meant, and no `allUsers` / `allAuthenticatedUsers` grant anywhere.
- `force_destroy` on the instance is left at its default of `false`.

## Tests

Added `tests/` — `terraform test` with `mock_provider`, 17 runs, no credentials
and no network. Coverage: `deletion_protection` defaults to `true`,
`num_nodes`/`processing_units` mutual exclusion, all the validation rejections,
and CMEK / PITR / drop-protection pass-through.

Proven to catch regressions: temporarily flipping the `deletion_protection`
default to `false` and reverting `local.effective_num_nodes` to an unconditional
`coalesce(var.num_nodes, 1)` produced `6 passed, 2 failed, 9 skipped`; restoring
both produced `17 passed, 0 failed`.

CI now runs `terraform test` and `tflint` alongside the existing OpenTofu
fmt/validate job.

## BREAKING

None of these change the resources produced by an existing configuration, but
they are behaviour changes worth reading before upgrading:

1. **`var.num_nodes` default changed from `1` to `null`.** The *effective*
   default is unchanged — omitting both `num_nodes` and `processing_units` still
   produces a one-node instance. But a caller who reads `num_nodes` back out of
   a `.tfvars`/wrapper and relied on the literal `1` will now see `null`.
2. **Setting both `num_nodes` and `processing_units` now fails at plan time.**
   Previously it reached the provider and failed at apply. This was always
   invalid; it just fails earlier and more clearly now.
3. **A database with both protections disabled now emits a plan warning.** It is
   a `check` block, so it is a warning during `plan`/`apply` and does not block
   anything. Note that `terraform test` escalates failed `check` assertions to
   errors, so a downstream test suite that deliberately disables both flags will
   go red until one is enabled.
4. **`examples/basic` is no longer destroyable in one step**, by design: set
   `deletion_protection = false`, apply, then destroy.

## How verified

```
terraform fmt -check -recursive     -> clean
terraform init -backend=false       -> hashicorp/google v7.41.0
terraform validate                  -> Success! The configuration is valid.
examples/basic: init + validate     -> Success! The configuration is valid.
terraform test                      -> Success! 17 passed, 0 failed.
tflint --recursive                  -> exit 0, no findings
```

Field availability was verified against the actual provider schemas rather than
assumed: `terraform providers schema -json` was diffed between
`hashicorp/google` 5.0.0 (the module's declared floor) and 7.41.0. Every
attribute used here — `processing_units`, `enable_drop_protection`,
`version_retention_period`, `database_dialect`, `encryption_config.kms_key_name`
— is present in 5.0.0, so `required_providers` did not need to be raised.
`deletion_policy`, `autoscaling_config`, `edition` and
`default_backup_schedule_type` are *not* in 5.0.0 and were deliberately not used.
